facts.label: Note
facts.value: Surrendered piecemeal in many separate agreements between 1764 and 1862. The data merges them into one area, so the whole area is shown until 1862.

facts.label: Shown here
facts.value: Only the parts not yet drawn as individual surrenders.

links.title: Upper Canada Land Surrenders (Crown–Indigenous Relations Canada)

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Mainly about 550–1200 CE, in the Late Woodland period; a few mounds are much older.

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Earthen mounds shaped like birds, bears, water spirits and other figures, built for ceremony and sometimes burial. The Ho-Chunk say the mounds were also places of refuge.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The area where effigy mounds are found, as the National Park Service describes it (quoted on Wikipedia): from Dubuque, Iowa, north into southeast Minnesota, across southern Wisconsin from the Mississippi to Lake Michigan, and along the Wisconsin–Illinois boundary.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 900 to 1650–1700 CE: Emergent (900–1000), Developmental (1000–1300) and Classic (1300–1650) horizons, then the historic period.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: the culture is believed to have transitioned into Siouan peoples of later times, such as the Ioway.

facts.label: Open questions
facts.value: Whether Oneota grew out of local Late Woodland cultures, came from elsewhere, or arose from contact with Mississippian peoples is not settled.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A guess at the 'Eastern Plains and Great Lakes area' the source gives: southern Wisconsin, southern Minnesota, Iowa, northern Missouri and northern Illinois. Oneota sites were not all occupied at once; communities moved over the centuries.

american-bottom-emergent.title: Late Woodland and Emergent Mississippian villages of the American Bottom

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Cahokia was a village of about 1,000 people before about 1050. Wikipedia calls about 900–1000 the Emergent Mississippian (or Terminal Late Woodland) period: summit buildings on platform mounds, shell-tempered pottery and wider trade.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The American Bottom, the Mississippi floodplain opposite St. Louis, with the bluffs beside it. Cahokia was settled here about 600 CE, in the Late Woodland period.

cahokia-height.title: Cahokia and the American Bottom at their height

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Cahokia grew quickly after about 1050, from perhaps 1,400–2,800 people to 10,200–15,300 by 1100 (a 2007 study cited on Wikipedia). It was most centralised in the Stirling phase, 1100–1200.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: At its peak, around 1100, the city covered about 4,000 acres with about 120 earthen mounds and nearly 20,000 people (Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The American Bottom from the mouth of the Illinois River to below St. Louis, with the uplands on either side: Cahokia, its East St. Louis and St. Louis precincts and the farming towns around them. Cahokia's influence reached much further (see Aztalan); that wider reach is not drawn.

facts.label: Decline
facts.value: By the middle of the 1200s Cahokia's population had fallen by half or more, and by 1350 the city was abandoned. Proposed causes include droughts and floods, the strain of feeding a large town, and political breakdown.

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: The wider region, the 'Vacant Quarter', had no large settlement from about 1400 to 1600, though work published in 2020 found the population rising again after 1400. The Illinois Confederation moved in in the mid-1600s; Wikipedia notes that the later Cahokia tribe was not necessarily descended from the Mississippian people.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The American Bottom only, as the population fell.

middle-mississippian-sphere.title: Mississippian towns of the central Mississippi valley, lower Ohio and Mid-South

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Mound towns here rose after about 1050. Many grew as people left the American Bottom during the droughts of the late 1100s and 1200s; the Nashville area peaked about 1275. Kincaid was occupied about 1050–1400 and Angel 1100–1450.

facts.label: The Vacant Quarter
facts.value: Wikipedia's Cahokia article calls the region around Cahokia the 'Vacant Quarter', with no settlement of any size from about 1400 to 1600 (though perhaps visited by hunting parties). This area is ended at about 1450, when Kincaid and Angel had both been abandoned, and left blank afterwards except where later towns are drawn.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A rough outline around the mound towns of the confluence region: southern Illinois (Kincaid), the lower Ohio (Angel), western Kentucky and Tennessee, the Nashville basin, the Tennessee River (Shiloh) and northeast Arkansas. Many separate chiefdoms, not one polity.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: People lived at Moundville from about 1000. Around 1150 its leaders began to rule a wider area; by 1300 it was the largest town in what is now Alabama. Between 1300 and 1450 the mounds fell out of use and most people moved to smaller sites nearby, using Moundville as a burial place.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: The Encyclopedia of Alabama says a gap in the written record makes it hard to link Moundville's people with historically known groups.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Black Warrior River valley for about 15 km either side of the river, from Tuscaloosa down past Moundville, where smaller one-mound centres stood along the river around the capital.

late-mississippian-st-francis.title: Late Mississippian towns of the St. Francis basin and around Memphis

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The Parkin phase dates from about 1400 to 1700.

facts.label: Contact
facts.value: Many archaeologists identify the Parkin phase with the province of Casqui and the Nodena phase with Pacaha, both visited by de Soto in 1541. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas describes heavily populated villages and wide maize fields in the 1540s, and a sparsely settled land by the 1670s.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: By the 1670s the area was home to the Quapaw, who spoke a Dhegiha Siouan language (Wikipedia, Parkin).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Northeast Arkansas and the Mississippi near Memphis: the Parkin phase villages on the St. Francis and Tyronza rivers and the neighbouring Nodena and Walls phases.

links.title: European Exploration and Settlement (Encyclopedia of Arkansas)

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: In Georgia the first chiefdoms formed in the Early Mississippian (800–1100); the Macon Plateau mounds at Ocmulgee date from about 950. In the Middle Mississippian (1100–1350) large chiefdoms ruled from great mound towns, the largest at Etowah. The Pee Dee people of the Carolinas emerged from about 980.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Georgia's river valleys, eastern Alabama, the Carolina Piedmont and the Pee Dee River, and the valleys of eastern Tennessee: a rough outline around Etowah, Ocmulgee and Town Creek.

south-appalachian-late.title: South Appalachian Mississippian: the paramount chiefdoms

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Late Mississippian (1350–1600): the large chiefdoms broke into smaller ones spread evenly along Georgia's valleys, later loosely joined into paramount chiefdoms such as Coosa, which had as many as seven member chiefdoms.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: New Georgia Encyclopedia: after European diseases and trade broke the chiefdoms, many remnant groups came together to form historically known peoples such as the Muscogee (Creeks), Cherokees and Seminoles.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A little wider than before, taking in the provinces the de Soto chronicles describe: Coosa in the southern Appalachians, Ocute in Georgia and Cofitachequi in South Carolina. Some valleys between them, such as the Savannah, were left as empty buffer zones; these are not cut out.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Sources differ: about 1200–1500 for the culture as a whole, while its largest centre, Lake Jackson, was occupied about 1050–1500. Local Weeden Island peoples took up maize farming and platform mounds from about 1000–1200; the later Leon-Jefferson phase ran into the contact period.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Fort Walton and later Leon-Jefferson peoples are the direct ancestors of the Apalachee.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: As the source defines it: from the Aucilla River west to Choctawhatchee Bay, and north into south Alabama and Georgia about 107 miles up the Apalachicola River and 50 miles up the Chattahoochee.

facts.label: Centre
facts.value: Bottle Creek, north of Mobile Bay, the largest Pensacola site and the largest on the Gulf Coast. Early Pensacola people were closely tied to Moundville upriver and may have come from there.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: As the source defines it: the Gulf Coast from Choctawhatchee Bay west to near Biloxi, most densely around Mobile Bay and the Mobile-Tensaw delta, and inland up the Tombigbee and Alabama rivers to about Selma. The eastern edge overlaps Fort Walton, as the source describes a transitional zone there.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 700–1200 CE, after the Troyville culture and before Plaquemine.

facts.label: What changed
facts.value: Population grew sharply. From about 800 people built two or three flat-topped mounds around a plaza to carry temples, and by 1000 simple elite polities had formed, though farming still rested on native seed crops rather than maize.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The lower Mississippi valley in Louisiana, western Mississippi and southeast Arkansas, with the Gulf Coast south of about Baton Rouge ('Coastal Coles Creek').

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 1200–1700 CE, growing out of Coles Creek. Plaquemine sites were still in use in the early 1700s.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Natchez and the related Taensa were the culture's historic-period descendants.

facts.label: Centres
facts.value: Ceremonial centres where mainly the elite lived, such as Winterville and Emerald, with most people on dispersed farmsteads.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: As the source defines it: the Mississippi valley from the Gulf to just south of the mouth of the Arkansas River, with the Yazoo basin and Natchez Bluffs in western Mississippi and the lower Ouachita and Red River valleys.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 650–1050 CE, in the Late Woodland period.

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: People stayed in the region but left the ceremonial centres. Wikipedia says their descendants are not known exactly; the Quapaw are responsible for Plum Bayou remains and objects under the federal repatriation law (NAGPRA).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: East-central Arkansas, in the uplands and floodplains of the White and Arkansas rivers around the Plum Bayou (Toltec) mounds.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Caddoan society began to take Mississippian form about 800 CE, grew out of the Fourche Maline and Mossy Grove cultures, and was distinctly 'Caddoan' by 1000. Major centres were Spiro on the Arkansas River and the Battle Mound site on the Red River.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: archaeological evidence shows unbroken continuity to the present, and Caddo speakers before and at European contact were the direct ancestors of the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The area the source names: eastern Oklahoma, western Arkansas, northeast Texas, southwest Missouri and northwest Louisiana, centred on the Arkansas and Red River valleys.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 1000–1750 CE. Around 1000 Late Woodland groups took up maize farming; by 1200 villages held up to 300 people around oval plazas; after 1400 villages grew larger and were often walled.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: the next people Europeans met in the area were the Shawnee, and scholars generally believe shared material culture, art, mythology and Shawnee oral history link them to Fort Ancient, though some evidence points the other way.

facts.label: Serpent Mound
facts.value: Radiocarbon dates tie the Great Serpent Mound and the Alligator Mound to the Fort Ancient era.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: As the source describes it: the middle Ohio valley in southern Ohio, western West Virginia, northern Kentucky and parts of southeast Indiana.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 1050–1635 CE. Villages of up to 50–100 houses moved from floodplains to fortified upland sites after about 1250.

facts.label: End
facts.value: The Monongahela disappear from the record in the 1620s or 1630s, before much direct contact with Europeans. Disease, war with the Haudenosaunee or Lenape, and severe droughts have all been proposed.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The upper Ohio basin as the source describes it: the Monongahela, Youghiogheny and Casselman valleys in western Pennsylvania, with neighbouring eastern Ohio, northern West Virginia and western Maryland.

facts.label: Why here
facts.value: Colonial pressure, then the Walking Purchase of 1737, pushed the Lenape west from the Delaware River; the Treaty of Easton (1758) required them to move on towards Ohio.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Allegheny valley from the Forks of the Ohio up past Kittanning, which the Lenape founded by 1724.

lenape-muskingum.title: Lenape towns on the Muskingum and Tuscarawas

facts.label: During the Revolution
facts.value: Some Lenape moved closer to Detroit, to the Scioto and Sandusky rivers; others stayed near Coshocton.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Around Coshocton, the main Lenape town, and the Moravian mission villages of Schoenbrunn, Gnadenhutten and Lichtenau on the Tuscarawas.

shawnee-scioto.title: Shawnee towns on the Scioto and Little Miami

facts.label: Return
facts.value: The Shawnee had been driven out of the region about 1660 in the Beaver Wars and returned from the east in the 1720s and after; about 400 moved from Pennsylvania in 1745. Lower Shawneetown had about 1,200 people by 1750.

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: Most Shawnee bands signed the Treaty of Greenville in 1795; the last Ohio Shawnee lands were ceded in 1817.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: From Lower Shawneetown at the mouth of the Scioto up the Scioto valley past Chalahgawtha (Chillicothe), and west to the Little Miami.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Both banks of the Detroit River, where Wendat and Petun descendants moved from Michilimackinac at Cadillac's invitation in 1701.

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: Reduced by the Treaty of Fort Meigs (1817) to the 7,680-acre Upper Sandusky Reservation, held until removal to Kansas in the 1840s.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: South of Sandusky Bay (Junundat, from 1738–39) and, after 1763, up the Sandusky River valley.

mingo-upper-ohio.title: Mingo towns on the upper Ohio River

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: Mingo also settled on the Sandusky River; most were removed to Kansas in 1832 and to Indian Territory in 1869.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Along the Ohio River below the Forks, where Mingo (mostly Seneca and Cayuga who had moved west from New York) settled in the mid-1700s. The extent is a guess.

miami-kekionga.title: Miami lands: Kekionga, the upper Wabash and the Great Miami

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: From Kekionga, the Miami capital at the head of the Maumee (now Fort Wayne), south-west along the upper Wabash and south-east to the Great Miami valley, where Pickawillany stood from 1747.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Basketmaker roots long before 800. Pueblo I and II (about 700–1130) saw fast growth; about 900–1150 was a 'golden age'. A long drought set in after about 1130. By about 1300 the Four Corners had been left (NPS: by 1300 at Navajo National Monument; the mid-1200s at Mesa Verde).

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: National Park Service (Mesa Verde): the Pueblo and Hopi people are the direct descendants of those who lived at Mesa Verde and the sites around it; they made new villages or joined others along the Rio Grande, the Little Colorado and on the Hopi mesas. Wikipedia: most modern Pueblo peoples say the Ancestral Puebloans did not vanish but moved and merged into today's Pueblos. The Hopi word for them is Hisatsinom.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: The older name 'Anasazi' is a Navajo word; contemporary Pueblos object to it, and many descendants prefer 'Ancestral Pueblo peoples' (Wikipedia).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The homeland Wikipedia describes: centred on the Colorado Plateau, from central New Mexico in the east to southern Nevada in the west; a loose northern edge in southern Nevada, Utah and Colorado; a southern edge along the Colorado and Little Colorado rivers in Arizona and the Rio Puerco and Rio Grande in New Mexico. Not every part was lived in at once: communities moved often, and the Chaco and Mesa Verde regions are drawn separately.

chaco-regional-system.title: Chaco Canyon and its great houses

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: NPS: the Chacoan flowering began in the mid-800s and lasted more than 300 years; Pueblo Bonito, Una Vida and Peñasco Blanco were built in the middle and late 800s. New building slowed in the 1100s and 1200s, and Chaco's influence carried on at Aztec, Mesa Verde and the Chuska Mountains.

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Planned stone 'great houses' of hundreds of rooms, aligned to the sun, moon and cardinal directions, and roads running for more than 180 miles (Wikipedia). NPS: they may have been public buildings used at times of ceremony and trade rather than farming villages.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: NPS: Pueblo descendants say Chaco was a special gathering place where many peoples and clans came together; Chaco is central to the origins of several Navajo clans and ceremonies; the people's descendants are the modern Southwest Indians. NPS lists 26 Pueblos and tribes as traditionally associated with Chaco.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The San Juan Basin, which the National Park Service says Chaco had become the centre of by 1050, with dozens of great houses in the canyon linked by roads to more than 150 great houses around the region. Drawn around the basin from the San Juan River to the Rio Puerco and the Chuska Mountains; the outlying great houses reached further than this.

mesa-verde-region.title: Mesa Verde region (northern San Juan) after Chaco

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: NPS: most of the cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde were built in the 1200s; life carried on until the mid-1200s, when people began to move south, and within a few decades the region was left entirely.

facts.label: Why people left
facts.value: NPS: persistent drought, limited resources and social change; for Pueblo people migration is an important cultural activity, and people may have decided it was time to move on and continue their journey.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: NPS: the Pueblo and Hopi people are the direct descendants of those who lived here; Ute, Navajo and Apache also call this place home, and Mesa Verde has 27 associated Pueblos and tribes.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southwest Colorado and southeast Utah between the Dolores and San Juan rivers, with the Aztec great houses on the Animas: the 'Mesa Verde region' and 'northern San Juan' the sources name, drawn from the rivers and mesas, not traced from a map (the NPS page has a map of the region, credited to Crow Canyon Archaeological Center, that has not been checked against). Hovenweep and Cedar Mesa are inside it.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Hohokam is dated about 300 to 1500 CE (Wikipedia) or 450 to 1450 (Archaeology Southwest). The Colonial or Preclassic period (about 750–1050/1150) was the time of ballcourts and of Snaketown at its height, in the early 1000s.

facts.label: Canals
facts.value: Irrigation canals on the Salt and Gila rivers, from 800 to 1400 among the most complex in the ancient world, the largest network in ancient North America (Archaeology Southwest); parts were renovated for Phoenix's water supply.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: NPS (Casa Grande): 'Hohokam' is an archaeologists' label, not the name of a tribe or people, and the builders were ancestors of the O'odham, Hopi and Zuni. Akimel O'odham elder Barnaby V. Lewis (Gila River Indian Community, via Archaeology Southwest): the O'odham word Huhugam means all O'odham ancestors, including those archaeologists call Hohokam.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Phoenix Basin along the Gila and lower Salt rivers (the Hohokam core) with the 'periphery' Wikipedia describes around it: Gila Bend in the west, the lower Verde to the north, the Tucson Basin and Santa Cruz valley to the south and east. A guess at the outer edge, which faded into neighbouring cultures.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Classic period about 1150–1450 (Wikipedia). Snaketown was abandoned early in it; pithouses gave way to walled compounds above ground, and platform mounds were built from about 1200. By 1300 Hohokam irrigation supported the largest population in the Southwest.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: As for the Preclassic: NPS calls the builders of Casa Grande ancestors of the O'odham, Hopi and Zuni; to the O'odham they are Huhugam, ancestors (Barnaby V. Lewis, via Archaeology Southwest).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Phoenix Basin, the middle Gila and the Tucson Basin, smaller than before: Wikipedia notes a major retraction of territory in the early Classic period. A guess at the outer edge.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Wikipedia: floods in the mid-1300s deepened the Salt River bed and broke the canal heads; after 1375 most villages and canals on the lower Salt were abandoned. Wikipedia calls this the aftermath of the Hohokam collapse and a critical stage in the forming of the modern O'odham.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Archaeology Southwest: the few people still living here in the 1400s are not counted as Hohokam by archaeologists, because their pottery, houses and customs had changed, but they were Huhugam, ancestors of the O'odham.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The middle Gila River and lower Queen Creek, where Wikipedia says the few villages that remained after 1375 were concentrated. A guess.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 200 CE to 1450 (or to the Spanish arrival in 1540). Pithouse villages until about 1000; surface pueblos from the 11th century; cliff dwellings in the 1200s and 1300s.

facts.label: Branches
facts.value: Mimbres, Jornada, Forestdale, Reserve, Point of Pines (Black River), San Simon and Upper Gila (Wikipedia).

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: contemporary Pueblo people claim descent from the Mogollon and related cultures; pottery traditions and oral history link Acoma, Hopi and Zuni to the Mogollon. The area was later lived in by the Apache, who are not related to the Mogollon.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southern New Mexico and southeast Arizona, northern Sonora and Chihuahua and west Texas, as Wikipedia gives the extent: from the Mogollon Rim and the Reserve area in the north to Casas Grandes in the south, and from the San Pedro valley in the west to the Jornada branch east of the Rio Grande (Three Rivers, Hueco Tanks). A guess at the outer edge; the Mimbres branch is drawn separately for its Classic phase.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Classic Mimbres phase about 1000–1130/1150, after the Three Circle phase (about 825–1000).

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Pueblos of up to 150 rooms around plazas near well-watered floodplains, and black-on-white bowls painted with geometric designs, animals and people, often buried with the dead. Looting of graves for these bowls has gone on since the 1960s.

facts.label: After 1150
facts.value: Wikipedia: the end of Classic Mimbres pottery was once read as the people 'disappearing'; more recent research finds the valley lost many people but some stayed, and people elsewhere changed their pottery and houses to resemble their neighbours'.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Mimbres Valley, the upper Gila and upper San Francisco rivers in southwest New Mexico and southeast Arizona, and the western side of the Rio Grande valley, as Wikipedia describes the Mimbres branch. Drawn inside the Mogollon sphere, which it is part of.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 500–1425 CE; fully developed sites from about 650. The eruptions of Sunset Crater in the 1060s spread ash that enriched the soil. The Verde Valley was left by the early 1400s; drought, worn-out land and conflict with newly arrived Yavapai have been suggested (Wikipedia).

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: several Hopi clans trace their ancestry to Sinagua immigrants who left the Verde Valley, they believe, for religious reasons; the National NAGPRA programme found evidence of continuity between the Verde Valley people of 1125–1425 and the Hopi Tribe. Pima, Tohono O'odham, Yavapai and Zuni may also have connections.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Central Arizona from the Little Colorado near Flagstaff to the Verde River near Sedona, with the Verde Valley, the country around the San Francisco Peaks and part of the Mogollon Rim, as Wikipedia gives it. Northern Sinagua around Flagstaff (Wupatki, Walnut Canyon), Southern Sinagua in the Verde Valley (Montezuma Castle, Tuzigoot).

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 1150 to the 1400s. The cliff dwellings now in Tonto National Monument were built in the 1300s by people who moved up from the crowded valley; about 1330 the valley grew drier (Wikipedia).

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Salado polychrome pottery, walled adobe compounds, burial rather than cremation, irrigated maize, cotton and beans, and copper bells cast in wax moulds.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: NPS (Tonto): the White Mountain, Chiricahua and Tonto Apache, Yavapai, Pima-Maricopa and others call this area home today, and many feel strong spiritual ties to the cliff dwellings, deeming them an ancestral home.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Tonto Basin and the upper Salt River (Wikipedia), with the Globe area. Salado pottery was traded and copied far beyond this; that wider reach is not drawn.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Wikipedia: Patayan ways of life lasted from about 700 to the 20th century; no clear end is drawn here, the area simply stops about 1500.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: From the Pai (Hualapai, Havasupai, Yavapai, Paipai) or Quechan word for 'old people' (Wikipedia gives both). Wikipedia says the historic Yuman-speaking peoples of this region were warriors and traders with networks reaching the Pima and the California coast; it does not say outright that they descend from the Patayan.

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Floodwater farming villages on the rivers, mobile hunting and gathering in the uplands, buff and brown pottery, and trade with the Hohokam.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The lower Colorado River valley and the lower Gila (as far upstream as the Painted Rock Mountains), with the uplands north toward the Grand Canyon and the Prescott area, as Wikipedia describes it; the culture reached west to Lake Cahuilla in California and into Baja California, outside this map's Southwest area. Little archaeological work has been done, so this is a guess.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: About 1 CE to 1300. Dean Snow (quoted on Wikipedia) dates a decline to about 950, after which people moved to the marshes of northwest Utah for about 400 years.

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: Part-time farmers of maize who also hunted and gathered, in scattered farmsteads and small villages, with grey pottery, distinctive basketry and rock art. Scholars do not agree that it was one people with one language.

facts.label: Later peoples
facts.value: Wikipedia: a 2000 study of mitochondrial DNA suggested that ancient Fremont people and modern Jemez Pueblo people share a maternal lineage. The Ute called the former people of the village ruins in their land 'mocutz'.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Most of Utah north of the Ancestral Puebloan country, with western Colorado and eastern Nevada, as Wikipedia gives it (the culture also reached into Idaho and Wyoming, outside this map's Southwest area). Range Creek, Nine Mile Canyon, the San Rafael Swell, Capitol Reef and Clear Creek Canyon are inside it.

athabaskan-route-utah.title: Proposed Southern Athabaskan route through the Great Basin and Utah

facts.label: Scholars' view
facts.value: Linguists and archaeologists hold that the Athabaskan (Dene) language family began in the north (Alaska and western Canada) and that the ancestors of the Navajo and Apache moved south, perhaps from about 1000 CE, reaching the Southwest between about 1200 and 1500; the dates, routes and number of migrations are debated (Wikipedia, Pearlstone, Archaeology 2020).

facts.label: Diné and Apache accounts
facts.value: Diné tradition places the people's emergence and homeland in Dinétah, within the four sacred mountains; many Navajo reject the migration theories because they contradict their oral history (Worley-Hood and Noyes 2013). Jicarilla Apache historian Veronica Tiller says the Apache too tell emergence stories based in the Southwest (Archaeology 2020). See the event 'Southern Athabaskan arrival: proposals and accounts'.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Not a territory: a band 60 km either side of a line from Promontory Caves on the Great Salt Lake, through central Utah, to the San Juan River and Dinétah, standing for one route scholars propose for the ancestors of the Navajo and Apache. Pearlstone (EBSCO) gives a mountain route 'by way of today's states of Utah or Colorado and the Great Basin'; the Apachean Origins Project dates moccasins at Promontory Caves to about 1250–1290. The line between those points is a guess; so are the dates the band is shown.

links.title: Athapaskans Arrive in the Southwest (EBSCO Research Starters)

athabaskan-route-rockies.title: Proposed Southern Athabaskan route along the Rocky Mountains

facts.label: Scholars' view
facts.value: Wikipedia: this theory has the ancestors of the Apache moving south through the Rocky Mountains and reaching the Southwest by the 14th century or earlier; an assemblage found in the mountains, the 'Cerro Rojo complex', has been called ancestral Apache, and the earliest evidence so far is in the mountainous Southwest. It does not rule out a Plains route as well. Wikipedia's Navajo article also says part of the migration ran along the Rocky Mountains.

facts.label: Diné and Apache accounts
facts.value: Many Navajo reject the migration theories because they contradict their oral history (Worley-Hood and Noyes 2013). See the event 'Southern Athabaskan arrival: proposals and accounts'.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Not a territory: a band 60 km either side of a line through the Colorado Rockies (North Park, the upper Arkansas, the San Luis Valley) to the Chama country, standing for the route 'south, through the Rocky Mountains' that Wikipedia describes, reaching the Southwest by the 1300s or earlier. The line itself is a guess; the sources name no valleys.

athabaskan-route-plains.title: Proposed Southern Athabaskan route along the western Plains

facts.label: Scholars' view
facts.value: Pearlstone (EBSCO): one possible reason for the move is that bison herds grew after the droughts of the 1400s and the Apacheans followed them south through the Plains, which would favour a route east of the Rockies; different groups may have used different routes. Wikipedia: the Plains theory links the Apache with the Dismal River culture (1675–1725) of Nebraska, Colorado and Kansas; archaeological data suggest Apache were on the Plains long before 1541.

facts.label: Diné and Apache accounts
facts.value: Many Navajo reject the migration theories because they contradict their oral history (Worley-Hood and Noyes 2013). See the event 'Southern Athabaskan arrival: proposals and accounts'.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Not a territory: a band 80 km either side of a line along the eastern foot of the Rockies, from the Wyoming border through eastern Colorado to the Llano Estacado, standing for the route through the northwestern and central Plains 'close to the eastern edge of the mountains' that Pearlstone (EBSCO) describes. It ends in 1541, when Coronado's expedition met the Querechos, bison hunters on these plains; the Apache Plains range is drawn from then. The line is a guess.

links.title: Athapaskans Arrive in the Southwest (EBSCO Research Starters)

dinetah-four-mountains.title: Dinétah, the Diné homeland within the four sacred mountains

facts.label: Diné tradition
facts.value: As summarised by Wikipedia and by Worley-Hood and Noyes (2013): the Diné emerged into this world through earlier worlds; the Holy People told them to keep the four sacred mountains as the bounds of a homeland they should never leave; the mountains and four rivers were made as protectors of the Diné. Dinétah means 'among the people'.

facts.label: Archaeology and Spanish records
facts.value: Wikipedia: growing evidence of Navajo presence in Dinétah from about 1500; archaeologists call about 1500–1630 the Dinétah phase and 1630–1800 the Gobernador phase. Spanish writers used 'Apachu de Nabajo' in the 1620s for people of the Chama region, and in the 1670s placed the Diné in Dinétah, about 60 miles west of the Chama.

facts.label: National Park Service
facts.value: Canyon de Chelly: related to the Athabaskan people of northern Canada and Alaska, the Navajo settled the Southwest between the four sacred mountains. Mesa Verde: the park sits just southwest of Dibé Nitsaa, the sacred mountain of the north, which marks the northern edge of the traditional Navajo homeland.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Straight lines between the four mountains that Diné tradition gives as the bounds of the homeland: Blanca Peak (Sisnaajiní) in the east, Mount Taylor (Tsoodził) in the south, the San Francisco Peaks (Dookʼoʼoosłííd) in the west and Hesperus Mountain (Dibé Nitsaa) in the north. Wikipedia says the bounds are inexact and marked by these peaks. Shown from 1500, the date archaeologists give for the earliest Navajo sites in Dinétah; in Diné tradition the homeland is older than any such date. Hopi, Pueblo and Ute lands lie partly inside it: lands were shared and contested.

links.title: Literature review of Utah Navajo land use (Utah Diné Bikéyah, 2013, PDF)

dinetah-heartland.title: Dinétah heartland (Largo, Carrizo, Blanco and Gobernador canyons to the Chama)

facts.label: Archaeology
facts.value: Wikipedia: archaeological finds thought to be proto-Navajo, in far northern New Mexico around the La Plata, Animas and Pine rivers, date to about 1500; dating is still debated, but it is generally agreed that the Navajo lived in Dinétah well before 1680. Small stone 'pueblitos', largely defensive, date to the late 1600s.

facts.label: Diné tradition
facts.value: Wikipedia: the region is where, in Diné tradition, the infant Changing Woman was found on Gobernador Knob, and where the first four Diné clans arrived after their migration from the north.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The canyons of the Largo and Carrizo washes south of the San Juan River, east and south of Farmington (Blanco, Largo, Carrizo and Gobernador canyons), which Wikipedia calls the heart of Dinétah, and east to the Chama valley, where Spanish writers placed the 'Apachu de Nabajo' in the 1620s. Overlaps the four-mountain homeland on purpose: this is where archaeology and Spanish records find the Diné, inside the land Diné tradition describes.

apache-plains-1541.title: Apache bison hunters of the southern Plains (Querechos)

facts.label: Spanish accounts
facts.value: Coronado (quoted on Wikipedia) described the Querechos as people who followed the bison, lived in well-made tents of tanned hides, and used dogs to carry their tents, poles and belongings. One camp had about two hundred tipis. Wikipedia says authorities agree the Querechos were Apache; its Apache article says possibly Plains Apache, at times maybe Navajo.

facts.label: Trade
facts.value: Wikipedia: when the Spanish arrived, the Pueblos traded maize and cotton cloth for bison meat, hides and stone with the Plains people, who wintered in camps near the Pueblos.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The plains east of the Pueblos, from the Canadian River to the Llano Estacado and the Pecos, where Coronado's expedition met the Querechos in 1541 after seventeen days' travel from the Pueblos. A guess: the Spanish accounts give no bounds.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Jicarilla were seminomadic in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and the plains of southern Colorado and northern New Mexico, ranged onto the Plains from before 1525, and in the 1600s farmed seasonally along the rivers, a practice learned from the Pueblos and the Spanish. Pearlstone (EBSCO): the Jicarilla settled in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado after parting from the Lipan.

facts.label: Shared places
facts.value: Wikipedia: Jicarilla stories name places shared with Taos Pueblo, and some shrines were shared with Taos.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The land between the four rivers the Jicarilla hold sacred, as Wikipedia gives them: the Rio Grande, Pecos, Arkansas and Canadian, in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado. They also ranged onto the Plains of Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas (not drawn). Shown from about 1600 because sources place them here 'in the 1600s'; exact dates are not known.

apache-east-1600.title: Apache east of the Rio Grande (later Mescalero)

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Pearlstone (EBSCO): the Mescalero settled east of the Chiricahua, reaching into Texas; the Apacheans were in these areas when the Spanish arrived. Wikipedia: the Mescalero hunted bison on the plains to the east and gathered mescal agave in the deserts to the south, from which the Spanish named them.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southeastern New Mexico and west Texas east of the Rio Grande: the Sierra Blanca, Sacramento, Organ and Guadalupe mountains, the Pecos valley and the Davis Mountains, where Wikipedia places the Mescalero groups. Their names in the sources come from after 1700 ('Faraones', a vague name before 1700); this is a guess at the 1600s.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Pearlstone (EBSCO): the Chiricahua and Mescalero were probably the last Apachean groups to part; the Chiricahua moved into southwest New Mexico, southeast Arizona and northern Mexico. Wikipedia: before 1722 Spanish writers used 'Apaches de Gila' for all Apacheans west of the Rio Grande, so early records seldom say which group is meant.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southwest New Mexico, southeast Arizona and northern Sonora and Chihuahua, from the San Pedro valley east to the Rio Grande and from near Magdalena south toward Ciudad Madera, as Wikipedia gives the Chiricahua range; drawn only as far south as this map's Southwest area. Wikipedia says the Chiricahua held about 15 million acres at the time of European contact; when that was for this region is not clear.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Pearlstone (EBSCO): the Western Apache and the Navajo moved west and south into the Four Corners region. Wikipedia: in 1540 Coronado called the modern Western Apache area uninhabited, though some scholars think he simply did not see the people; Spanish explorers first mention 'Querechos' west of the Rio Grande in the 1580s.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: East-central Arizona: the White Mountains, the Mogollon Rim and the upper Salt and Gila rivers south to the Pinaleño Mountains, the core of the range Wikipedia gives the Western Apache (which also reached the Little Colorado and, for the Tonto groups, the upper Verde). A guess at the 1600s.

facts.label: Hopi Tribe
facts.value: Since time immemorial the Hopi people have lived in Hopitutskwa and kept their sacred covenant with Maasaw, caretaker of the earth, to live as peaceful and humble farmers.

facts.label: Villages
facts.value: Wikipedia: Old Oraibi was founded about 1100; Awatovi after 1300. In 1540 the Spanish recorded five Hopi villages; Oraibi alone had 1,500–3,000 people. NPS (Canyon de Chelly): the Hopi, descendants of the Puebloans, also farmed in Canyon de Chelly before settling on the mesas.

facts.label: 1680–1700
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Hopi joined the Pueblo Revolt and, alone among the Pueblos, stayed free of Spanish rule after 1692.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Hopi mesas with Antelope Mesa and the Homol'ovi villages on the Little Colorado, the cluster Wikipedia describes around Awatovi after 1300. Hopi land (Hopitutskwa) was wider than this; the outline is only the core of villages and fields. Before 1300 the area is inside the Ancestral Puebloan sphere.

zuni-1300.title: Zuni villages (Halona Idiwan'a, the Middle Place)

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Wikipedia: Zuni ancestors farmed the Zuni River valley from the last millennium BCE; Zuni culture is linked with both Mogollon and Ancestral Puebloan cultures. In the 1300s the Zuni lived in about a dozen pueblos; they later moved from the east to the west of their land and built six new villages. Only Halona was still lived in by 1700.

facts.label: Name
facts.value: The Zuni call their homeland Halona Idiwan'a, the Middle Place (Wikipedia).

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Zuni River valley and the land around the six villages of the 1400s–1600s (Halona, Hawikku, Kyaki:ma, Matsaki, Kwakina and Kechiba:wa), with Dowa Yalanne. Zuni use of the land reached much further; this is the core of villages and fields.

facts.label: Pueblo of Acoma
facts.value: Acoma's establishment was first recorded in 1150, and it is called the oldest continuously inhabited community in North America (Sky City Cultural Center).

facts.label: Wikipedia
facts.value: Pueblo people descend from Ancestral Puebloans, Mogollon and other peoples. Archaeologists say Acoma had emerged by the 13th century; the Acoma say Sky City was founded in the 11th century. After 1680 some who left Acoma helped form Laguna Pueblo.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A rough outline around the Acoma mesa and the valleys and farming villages near it, between Mount Taylor and the Rio San José; not the full Acoma land base. Before 1300 the area is inside the Ancestral Puebloan sphere; Acoma's own record of its founding is older (see the Acoma event).

links.title: Acoma Then & Now (Sky City Cultural Center)

rio-grande-pueblos-1300.title: Pueblos of the Rio Grande, Pecos, Galisteo and Salinas

facts.label: Who
facts.value: NPS: when people left Mesa Verde they made new villages or joined others along the Rio Grande. Wikipedia: by 1680 there were 46 Pueblo towns, speaking Northern Tiwa (Taos, Picuris), Tewa (Ohkay Owingeh, Santa Clara, San Ildefonso, Nambé, Pojoaque, Tesuque), Towa (Jemez, Pecos), Tano (Galisteo), Keres (Cochiti, Kewa, San Felipe, Santa Ana, Zia), Southern Tiwa (Sandia, Isleta and the Tiguex towns) and Piro.

facts.label: After 1540
facts.value: Wikipedia: Coronado's expedition fought the Tiwa in 1540–41; Oñate set up the colony in 1598. The Salinas pueblos were empty of both Pueblo and Spanish people by the late 1670s. In 1680 the Southern Tiwa and Piro did not join the revolt, and the Piro left with the Spanish for El Paso.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Rio Grande valley from Taos to the Piro towns below Socorro, with the Chama, the Jemez valley, the Pajarito Plateau, the Galisteo Basin, Pecos and the Salinas pueblos east of the Manzano Mountains. Rough; the Pueblos' farmed and hunted lands reached into the mountains around.

rio-grande-pueblos-1680.title: Pueblos of the Rio Grande after the Revolt

facts.label: 1680–1700
facts.value: Wikipedia: after the revolt the Pueblos governed themselves for twelve years. Vargas returned in 1692 and retook Santa Fe by force in 1693; after a second revolt in 1696 was put down, many Pueblo people left to join the Apache or Navajo or to settle on the Plains; Picuris people under Luis Tupatu went to their Jicarilla allies at El Cuartelejo in Kansas. The Spanish then granted land to each Pueblo.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: As before, without the Piro towns south of Isleta and the Salinas pueblos, which had been left by 1680. Many people moved in these years (to mesa-top refuges, to the Hopi, Navajo and Apache, and to the Plains), and that is not drawn.

facts.label: Ancestors
facts.value: Barnaby V. Lewis (Akimel O'odham, via Archaeology Southwest): O'odham oral tradition identifies the Huhugam as the ancestral relatives of today's O'odham. Wikipedia: most archaeologists believe the O'odham descend from the Hohokam, though some argue one group moved into the other's land.

facts.label: Spanish records
facts.value: Father Kino found the great house at Casa Grande abandoned in 1694 (Wikipedia); the O'odham word Huhugam was first written down in that year (Archaeology Southwest). Wikipedia lists O'odham rancherías in the Santa Cruz valley in the late 1600s.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Sonoran Desert of southern and central Arizona, Wikipedia's 'historical territory' of the O'odham: the Gila and Salt rivers (Akimel O'odham, the River People) and the desert to the south and west (Tohono O'odham); it also reached into northern Sonora, outside this map's Southwest area. No source read gives the bounds for the 1400s–1600s; Spanish records begin in the 1690s.

ute-1300.title: Ancestral Ute (southwest Colorado and southeast Utah)

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Southern Numic speakers (Ute and Southern Paiute) were the first to leave the Numic homeland near the Nevada–California border; there were ancestral Utes in southwest Colorado and southeast Utah by 1300. NPS (Mesa Verde): the Ute call themselves mountain people; bands moved between high summer and low winter country, and Mesa Verde was one of their hunting and gathering grounds.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southwest Colorado and southeast Utah, where Wikipedia says there were ancestral Utes by 1300, living by hunting and gathering. The outline is a guess.

facts.label: Sources
facts.value: Wikipedia: the Utes occupied much of present Colorado by the 1600s; the Comanche joined them in eastern Colorado in the early 1700s. Winter camps were along rivers near today's Provo and Fort Duchesne in Utah and Pueblo, Fort Collins and Colorado Springs in Colorado.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Most of Utah, western and central Colorado and the San Juan watershed in New Mexico, the area Wikipedia says the Utes came to live in; it says they held much of Colorado by the 1600s. Hunting grounds reached further (not drawn). Southern Paiute, Shoshone and Goshute lands in the west and north of Utah are not yet drawn, so the western edge is a guess.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 9 May 1781, with Chippewa and Mississauga chiefs

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A strip about four miles wide on the west side of the Niagara River, from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 9 October 1783, on Carleton Island, negotiated by Captain William Crawford

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The north shore of Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence from near Gananoque west to the Trent River, about 30 miles inland, with the islands.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Bought in May 1784 so that the Crown could grant the Grand River to the Six Nations; confirmed by Treaty No. 3, 7 December 1792

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The land between Lakes Ontario and Erie, from the Niagara west to the Thames (La Tranche) and Catfish Creek, including the Grand River valley.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 19 May 1790, with the Ottawa, Chippewa, Potawatomi and Huron (Wyandot) of Detroit

facts.label: Kept back
facts.value: Reserves including Bois Blanc Island and the Huron Church lands on the Detroit River

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: From Catfish Creek on Lake Erie west to the Detroit River, and north to the Chenail Ecarté and the Thames (La Tranche).

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: First agreed 23 September 1787; the deed was redone on 1 August 1805 because the first was defective

facts.label: Settlement
facts.value: In 2010 Canada agreed to pay the Mississaugas of the Credit CA$145 million for this and nearby lands

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: From Etobicoke Creek east to about Ashbridge's Bay, and about 28 miles north towards Lake Simcoe.

facts.label: Kept back
facts.value: Reserves on the Credit River and Sixteen and Twelve Mile Creeks

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 85,000 acres along Lake Ontario between Etobicoke Creek and Burlington Bay, bounded inland by Brant's lands.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 17–18 November 1815, with Chippewa chiefs Kinaybicoinini, Aisaince and Misquuckkey

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 250,000 acres between Kempenfelt Bay on Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay, including Nottawasaga, Matchedash and Sturgeon Bays: the old Wendat country.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 17 October 1818, with Chippewa chiefs including Musquakie

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 1,592,000 acres bounded by Georgian Bay, Lake Simcoe, Kempenfelt Bay and the Holland River.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 28 October 1818, with Mississauga chiefs including Adjutant (Ajetance)

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 648,000 acres inland from the 1806 lakeshore purchase, including the upper Credit River and Twelve and Sixteen Mile Creeks.

facts.label: Names
facts.value: The treaty text calls the signatories Chippewa. The Paudash account describes the people of the Trent valley and Rice Lake as Mississauga.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 1,951,000 acres east of Lake Simcoe, including Rice Lake and the Trent and Talbot Rivers, inland from the lakeshore townships.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 8 July 1822, with Chippewa chiefs including Tummago

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 580,000 acres on the north side of the Thames, from London Township west towards Chatham.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 28 November 1822, with Mississauga chiefs including Nawacamigo

facts.label: Note
facts.value: This land lies within the area of the Algonquins of Ontario land claim; Algonquins were not party to the purchase.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 2,748,000 acres behind the St. Lawrence front townships, reaching north to the Ottawa River.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 10 July 1827, with Chippewa chiefs including Wawanosh

facts.label: Kept back
facts.value: Reserves at the Aux Sable River, Kettle Point, the St. Clair River and in Sombra, 17,951 acres in all

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: About 2,182,000 acres along Lake Huron and the St. Clair River, north of the Long Woods purchase.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 9 August 1836, proposed by Sir Francis Bond Head: the Saugeen people were to move to Manitoulin Island or north of Owen Sound

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Saugeen territory south of a line from the Saugeen River to Owen Sound.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: 13 October 1854, with the Saugeen and Owen Sound chiefs

facts.label: Kept back
facts.value: Reserves at Saugeen, Chief's Point, Owen Sound, Cape Croker and Colpoy's Bay; the islands were excluded

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Bruce (Saugeen) Peninsula between Lake Huron and Georgian Bay, north of the 1836 line.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: In 1836 the island was set aside as a refuge for Native people; on 6 October 1862 it was released to the Crown and opened to settlement

facts.label: Kept back
facts.value: Grants of 100 acres per head of family and 50 per single adult

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Manitoulin Island and nearby islands, except the north-east peninsula, Wiikwemkoong, which was not ceded.

facts.label: Never ceded
facts.value: Two bands living here said that the chiefs who signed the 1862 treaty did not represent them; their land was left out of the cession and has never been surrendered.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The north-east peninsula of Manitoulin Island.

facts.label: Lost
facts.value: Joseph Brant sold 381,480 acres, the northern half, to private buyers in the 1790s; the Crown sold the land in six blocks on 5 February 1798, later Dumfries, Waterloo, Woolwich, Nichol and other townships.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Six miles each side of the Grand River, from about Paris north to Fergus. The grant ran to the river's head, but the Crown later held that it reached only as far as the land it had bought.

facts.label: Granted
facts.value: 25 October 1784, by the Haldimand Proclamation, to the Mohawk and other Six Nations people

facts.label: Lost
facts.value: Surrenders in 1841 and 1844 opened the land to sale. Six Nations petitioned against the 1841 surrender, saying the chiefs had been intimidated and had agreed only to a lease. In 1850 the reserve was set at about 47,000 acres.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Six miles each side of the Grand River, from Lake Erie up to about Paris.

six-nations-reserve.title: Six Nations of the Grand River reserve

facts.label: Size
facts.value: About 47,000 acres, set in 1850: roughly 5% of the Haldimand Tract

facts.label: Today
facts.value: Six Nations' claims over the lost land are before the courts; land defence continues.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A rough outline around Ohsweken, south-east of Brantford, of about the reserve's size; not its surveyed boundary.

wendake.title: Wendake, homeland of the Wendat confederacy

facts.label: Dispersal
facts.value: Haudenosaunee attacks in 1648–49 led the Wendat to abandon their villages; refugees wintered on Gahoendoe (Christian Island) in 1649–50.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The country between Nottawasaga Bay, Matchedash Bay and Lake Simcoe, the area the cited works call Huronia. The Wendat had lived here long before 1600.

facts.label: Dispersal
facts.value: Destroyed as a nation by the Haudenosaunee wars by about 1650–52; survivors joined Wendat refugees.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: South and west of Nottawasaga Bay, around the Blue Mountains, beside Wendake.

facts.label: Dispersal
facts.value: The Haudenosaunee went to war with the Neutral about 1650; they dispersed in 1651.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The heartland from the Grand River to the Niagara River, including the Niagara Peninsula and the Hamilton–Milton area, with the cluster of villages east of the Niagara near Buffalo. Villages also stood further west (London, St. Thomas, near Windsor); that wider range is not drawn.

facts.label: Dispersal
facts.value: Defeated by Seneca and Onondaga warriors in 1654–56; most survivors were absorbed into Haudenosaunee communities.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The south-east shore of Lake Erie between the Buffalo River and Presque Isle Bay, on the Erie Plain. French maps of 1650 show the Erie along the whole south shore, but archaeologists place them only in this eastern part.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The Mohawk Valley, the easternmost of the Five Nations' village areas. Hunting grounds reached much further, into the Adirondacks and beyond; they are not drawn.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: South and east of Oneida Lake, between the Mohawk and Onondaga village areas. Hunting grounds reached further; they are not drawn.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Around Onondaga Lake and south of it, the central nation of the Confederacy. Hunting grounds reached further; they are not drawn.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Around Cayuga Lake. Hunting grounds reached further; they are not drawn.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: From Seneca Lake west to the Genesee River, the westernmost of the Five Nations' village areas. After the 1650s the Seneca also used lands further west; those are not drawn.

haudenosaunee-north-shore.title: Haudenosaunee villages on the north shore of Lake Ontario

facts.label: Villages
facts.value: Quinaouatoua (near Hamilton), Teiaiagon (Humber River), Ganatsekwyagon (Rouge River), Ganaraske (Port Hope), Kentsio (Rice Lake), Kente (Bay of Quinte), Ganneious (near Napanee)

facts.label: Abandoned
facts.value: After Denonville's French force destroyed Kente and Ganneious in June 1687; Teiaiagon's Seneca left by about 1701.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: A band along the north shore from Quinaouatoua near Hamilton to Ganneious near Napanee, taking in the seven village sites and the portages inland to Lake Simcoe and Rice Lake. How far inland the villages' lands reached is a guess.

odawa-homeland.title: Odawa homeland: Manitoulin Island and the Bruce Peninsula

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Manitoulin Island and the Bruce Peninsula, which the Odawa regard as their original homeland. Champlain met them near the mouth of the French River in 1615. After 1701 many moved to Detroit and northern Michigan.

facts.label: Note
facts.value: Some Nipissing moved to the Lake Nipigon area during the 1600s and later returned.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Around Lake Nipissing, on the canoe route between the Ottawa River and Georgian Bay.

ojibwe-north-shore.title: Ojibwe and Mississauga lands on the north shore of Lake Huron

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: The north shore of Lake Huron from Sault Ste. Marie east to the French River, including the Mississagi River, from which the Mississauga take their name and from which the Paudash account says they came south.

algonquin-ottawa-valley.title: Algonquin (Omàmiwininì) lands in the Ottawa Valley

facts.label: Never ceded
facts.value: Much of this land was never surrendered by treaty. The Algonquins of Ontario land claim, open since 1983, covers the Ontario side; an agreement-in-principle of 2015 is disputed by many Algonquins.

facts.label: Note
facts.value: Haudenosaunee raids in the 1640s scattered several bands; this area is shown continuously because the land itself was not given up.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Both sides of the Ottawa River (Kitcisìpi), from Lake Nipissing's outlet towards Montreal, where the Kichesipirini, Weskarini, Matàwackariniwak and other Algonquin bands lived.

anishinaabe-southern-ontario.title: Mississauga and Ojibwe lands in southern Ontario

facts.label: Afterwards
facts.value: From 1764 these lands were surrendered piecemeal to the Crown in the Upper Canada Land Surrenders.

facts.label: How this area was drawn
facts.value: Southern Ontario from the Detroit River and Lake Huron east along the north shores of Lakes Erie and Ontario to the St. Lawrence near Brockville. Rogers dates the move south to the 1690s, with Ojibwe in the Niagara region by about 1707; the Paudash account names the Trent valley and the St. Lawrence as far as Brockville.
