sites.label: Cahokia Mounds, Collinsville, Illinois (Monks Mound)

accounts.summary: A Late Woodland village from about 600, Cahokia grew very fast after about 1050 into a city of three precincts and about 120 earthworks. Its population peaked around 1100 at perhaps 15,000–20,000. It had halved by the mid-1200s, and the city was abandoned by 1350.

The largest pre-Columbian site north of Mexico. At its peak around 1100 the city spread over about 4,000 acres with about 120 mounds and nearly 20,000 people. The state protects about 2,200 acres of the centre; the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

sites.label: Aztalan State Park, Crawfish River, Wisconsin

accounts.summary: A walled Mississippian town with earthen mounds on the Crawfish River, far to the north of Cahokia, with copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf. Wikipedia's article on the site says it was first settled about 900; its article on the Mississippian period counts it among the outposts Cahokians set up in the north between 1050 and 1100. Woodland traditions are also found there, and Oneota people lived at the site for a time. It was abandoned between 1200 and 1300.

sites.label: Kincaid Mounds, Ohio River, Massac and Pope counties, Illinois

accounts.summary: A Mississippian town and trading centre on the Ohio River, about 140 miles from Cahokia, with at least 11 platform mounds. Late Woodland people had lived there before. Excavations by the University of Chicago in 1934–41 trained many later archaeologists.

sites.label: Angel Mounds, near Evansville, Indiana

accounts.summary: The walled capital of a chiefdom on the Ohio River, with thirteen mounds and up to about 1,000 people inside its palisade. Wikipedia's article on the Mississippian period says it was founded partly by people from Cahokia, or by priests trained there, and took in migrants as Cahokia declined.

sites.label: Shiloh Indian Mounds, Tennessee River, Hardin County, Tennessee

accounts.summary: A palisaded town on a bluff over the Tennessee River, with seven platform mounds, a burial mound and over a hundred houses, the centre of a chiefdom along about 20 miles of the valley. Lived in from about 1000 by Late Woodland and then Early Mississippian people; abandoned about 1350. Wikipedia's article on the Mississippian period says migrants from Shiloh and the Tennessee valley helped found Moundville.

moundville.title: Moundville
moundville.when: about 1150–1450 as a regional capital (lived in from about 1000)

sites.label: Moundville Archaeological Park, Black Warrior River, Alabama

accounts.summary: A walled town of 29 mounds around a plaza, the largest in what is now Alabama by 1300, with perhaps 1,000 people inside and more on farms along the river. Between 1300 and 1450 the mounds fell out of use and people moved to smaller sites nearby; Moundville became mainly a burial place. By de Soto's march in 1540 it likely had few people, and none of the towns the chroniclers name can be identified with it for certain.
The second-largest site of the classic Mississippian era after Cahokia. Its leaders began to rule a wider area around 1150; by 1500 most of the site was abandoned.

sites.label: Etowah Indian Mounds, Etowah River, near Cartersville, Georgia

accounts.summary: A 54-acre town with at least six mounds around two plazas, the largest a temple mound just over 60 feet high, protected by a ditch and a palisade with bastions. Settled by the 1100s, and by many archaeologists' dating two centuries earlier, it was lived in with short breaks into the 1600s. In the Middle Mississippian (1100–1350) it was the largest chiefdom capital in Georgia.

Built and occupied in three phases from 1000 to 1550 by a series of chiefdoms. Wikipedia says its builders were ancestors of the Muscogee (Creek), and that the Muscogee and the Cherokee, who each lived in the area at different times, hold the site sacred. The town of Itaba that de Soto's expedition passed in 1540 was likely Etowah.

sites.label: Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park, Macon, Georgia

accounts.summary: The main occupation of the Macon Plateau, about 950–1150, built the Great Temple Mound, 55 feet high, with other platform mounds and earth lodges; one earth lodge is dated to about 1050. Archaeologists call this the Macon Plateau culture, a local form of South Appalachian Mississippian. Later, Lamar-period people (from about 1350) built mounds downriver.
The park preserves more than 12,000 years of continuous human habitation and is the ancestral homeland of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, who live in Oklahoma today.

sites.label: Town Creek Indian Mound, near Mount Gilead, North Carolina

accounts.summary: A ceremonial centre of the Pee Dee people, with a 15-foot platform mound built over an earth lodge, a village and a palisade. It was abandoned for reasons not known. It is the only Pee Dee mound centre in North Carolina.

sites.label: Lake Jackson Mounds, Tallahassee, Florida

accounts.summary: Capital of a Fort Walton chiefdom, with seven mounds; burials in Mound 3 held copper plates and engraved shell like those of Etowah. About 1500 the chiefdom's seat moved to Anhaica, where de Soto's army met the Apalachee and spent the winter of 1539–40.

links.title: Lake Jackson Mounds Archaeological State Park (Wikipedia)

sites.label: Winterville Mounds, near Greenville, Mississippi

accounts.summary: A Plaquemine ceremonial centre with more than twelve platform mounds, mostly built between 1200 and 1250. Only leading families lived there; most people farmed across the Yazoo delta. It was abandoned by 1450.

sites.label: Emerald Mound, Natchez Trace Parkway, near Stanton, Mississippi

accounts.summary: The second-largest Mississippian mound in the United States after Monks Mound at Cahokia: 35 feet high, covering eight acres, with two smaller mounds on top. It was built and used between about 1200 and 1730. Nearly all the towns de Soto's men saw were abandoned by the late 1600s, but the people did not disappear; they adapted to the loss.
Built between about 1250 and 1600 around a natural hill; the historic Natchez still used it as their main ceremonial centre until the late 1730s.

sites.label: Parkin Archeological State Park, St. Francis River, Arkansas

accounts.summary: A palisaded village where the Tyronza meets the St. Francis, type site of the Late Mississippian Parkin phase. Many archaeologists think it was the main town of Casqui, which de Soto visited in 1541; a Spanish glass bead, bells and musket balls have been found there.

sites.label: Plum Bayou Mounds Archeological State Park, near Scott, Arkansas

accounts.summary: An 18-mound Late Woodland centre on an oxbow of the Arkansas River, with the tallest surviving prehistoric mounds in Arkansas, used from the 600s to the 1000s. The old name 'Toltec' came from a 19th-century mistake that linked the mounds to Mexico.

links.title: Plum Bayou Mounds Archeological State Park (Wikipedia)

sites.label: Spiro Mounds, Arkansas River, Le Flore County, Oklahoma

accounts.summary: A religious and political centre of the Arkansas valley Caddoan people from the 800s to the 1400s, and a major western centre of the Mississippian world, linked to what archaeologists call the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex. In the 1930s treasure hunters tunnelled into Craig Mound, found a hollow burial chamber full of rare objects, including textiles and feathers, and sold them to collectors.

sites.label: Not known: somewhere in central Alabama. One proposal is southwest of Selma; finds announced in 2021 in Marengo County may mark the province of Mabila (marker approximate)

accounts.summary: De Soto had taken the paramount chief Tuskaloosa hostage, demanding bearers and women. Tuskaloosa led the Spaniards to Mabila, a palisaded town where warriors waited hidden in the houses. After a Spaniard struck a man there, fighting broke out; the Spaniards were driven out, then set the town on fire. By the chronicler Elvas's count about 200 Spaniards died in the nine-hour fight, 150 were badly wounded, and 20 more died in the following weeks.

Estimates of the Native dead run from about 2,000 to 6,000, making it one of the bloodiest battles in recorded North American history. The Spaniards lost most of their supplies and turned inland rather than meet their ships on the coast. The town's site is still sought.

chicaza-1541.title: Chickasaw attack on de Soto's camp

sites.label: De Soto's winter camp in inland Mississippi, most likely near Tupelo (approximate)

accounts.summary: After wintering near present-day Tupelo, de Soto demanded 200 men from the Chickasaw to carry the expedition's loads. They refused and attacked the Spanish camp by night.

sites.label: Casqui, probably the Parkin site, Arkansas

accounts.summary: Casqui welcomed de Soto, whose men raised a cross on its mound. Casqui and its neighbour Pacaha had long been at war; Casqui warriors who followed the Spaniards to Pacaha sacked the town. When de Soto threatened to help Pacaha punish them, Casqui returned the goods and apologised, and de Soto brought the two chiefs to a dinner where they made peace. The expedition's journals are the only written record of Casqui.

De Soto's force crossed the Mississippi on 18 June 1541, the first Europeans in what is now Arkansas, and found large towns such as Pacaha and Casqui in the northeast. The Spaniards killed many people, took food stores, and upset the region's politics, weakening some chiefs and backing others.

links.title: European Exploration and Settlement (Encyclopedia of Arkansas)

pueblo-bonito.title: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon
pueblo-bonito.when: built from the mid-800s; lived in about 828–1126

sites.label: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Culture National Historical Park, New Mexico

accounts.summary: One of the first great houses, built in the middle and late 800s. By 1050 Chaco was the ceremonial, administrative and economic centre of the San Juan Basin. Pueblo descendants say Chaco was a gathering place where many peoples and clans shared ceremonies and knowledge; many Southwest Indian people see it as a stop on their clans' sacred migration paths. Chaco is also central to the origins of several Navajo clans and ceremonies.

The largest and best-known great house, with about 700 rooms in up to five storeys, built in stages and lived in about 828–1126. A crypt in Room 33 held one powerful family line, traced through the female line, for about 330 years. The Chacoans left the canyon probably because of a 50-year drought that began in 1130.

sites.label: Aztec Ruins National Monument, Animas River, New Mexico

accounts.summary: Great houses on the Animas River built by Ancestral Puebloans in the 12th and 13th centuries, part of the Chaco Culture World Heritage Site. Nineteenth-century settlers named them 'Aztec' in the mistaken belief that the Aztecs had built them.
As new building slowed at Chaco in the 1100s and 1200s, Chaco's influence carried on at Aztec, Mesa Verde and other centres to the north, south and west.

sites.label: Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde National Park, Colorado

accounts.summary: The largest cliff dwelling in the park, with 150 rooms and 23 kivas and about 100 people, perhaps a social, administrative and ceremonial centre. Three quarters of the park's 600-odd cliff dwellings have only one to five rooms. Laguna Pueblo's TJ Atsye, quoted by the park: 'Even though we physically moved away, the spirits of my ancestors are still here.'
Built and lived in from about 1200 to 1300, and left by 1300; why is still debated, and some point to a series of megadroughts.

sites.label: Snaketown, Hohokam Pima National Monument, Gila River Indian Community, near Sacaton, Arizona (approximate; closed to the public)

accounts.summary: The leading Preclassic Hohokam town, with two ballcourts, a central plaza, large community houses and hundreds of pithouses for several thousand people. At its height in the early 1000s it was the centre of Hohokam buff-ware pottery. It was suddenly abandoned early in the Classic period, partly burned, and never lived in again. Excavated in the 1930s and 1960s and then reburied.

accounts.perspective: Gila River Indian Community (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The site is owned by the Gila River Indian Community, which has chosen not to open it to the public; the nearby Huhugam Heritage Center has exhibits on tribal history and archaeology.

sites.label: Casa Grande Ruins National Monument, Coolidge, Arizona

accounts.summary: Built by ancestral Sonoran Desert people who farmed with wide-scale irrigation and traded far for over a thousand years, until about 1450, when the great house went out of use. 'Hohokam' is an archaeologists' label, not the name of a people; years of misunderstanding have confused the ancestors of the O'odham, Hopi and Zuni with that name. Father Kino named the ruin 'casa grande' in 1694.

accounts.perspective: Akimel O'odham oral tradition (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: Traditions recorded by Frank Russell in the early 1900s say the great house was built by an important leader, Sial Teu-utak Sivan ('Turquoise Leader'), and call the place Sivan Vahki. The O'odham word Huhugam was first written down in 1694, when the Spanish came to Sivan Vahki (Archaeology Southwest).

sites.label: Paquimé, Casas Grandes, Chihuahua, Mexico

accounts.summary: A town of house clusters around plazas with a shared water system, rebuilt after a fire about 1340 as multi-storey adobe blocks of about 2,000 rooms, with Mesoamerican-style ballcourts, platforms, effigy mounds and workshops for copper bells and shell beads. Perhaps 2,500 people lived there and 10,000 in the area it controlled. Its pottery was traded north into New Mexico and Arizona. It is credited to the Mogollon culture; Stephen Lekson's idea that Chaco's rulers moved on to Aztec and then Paquimé is not widely accepted. Abandoned about 1450.

sites.label: Wupatki Pueblo, Wupatki National Monument, near Flagstaff, Arizona

accounts.summary: A pueblo of over 100 rooms with a community room and the northernmost ballcourt known in North America, built by Ancestral Puebloan groups (Cohonina, Kayenta and Sinagua). Many people moved in after Sunset Crater erupted in the 11th century and its ash improved the soil. About 85–100 people lived there by 1182; it was left for good by 1225. Wupatki means 'Long Cut House' in Hopi.

sites.label: Montezuma Castle National Monument, Beaver Creek, Camp Verde, Arizona

accounts.summary: One of the best preserved cliff dwellings in North America, made one of the first four national monuments in 1906. The Sinagua lived in this green 'oasis' along Beaver Creek for over 400 years.

Built as early as 1125 and lived in until as late as 1395, by the people archaeologists call Southern Sinagua. Many Native communities trace their ancestry to people who lived here; they may define that ancestry differently from archaeologists, and may prefer their own words to archaeological labels. Several Hopi clans trace their ancestry to people of the Verde Valley.

tonto-cliff-dwellings.title: Tonto cliff dwellings
tonto-cliff-dwellings.when: built in the 1300s; the Salado culture lasted into the 1400s

sites.label: Lower and Upper Cliff Dwellings, Tonto National Monument, Arizona

accounts.summary: Two cliff dwellings of mud and stone, built in the 1300s in recesses in the hills above the Tonto Basin by Salado people who moved up from the crowded valley. The Lower Cliff Dwelling had sixteen ground-floor rooms and an annex of twelve; the Upper had thirty-two. The valley villages now lie under Theodore Roosevelt Lake.

The Tonto Basin has been home to many peoples for nearly 10,000 years. The White Mountain, Chiricahua and Tonto Apache, Yavapai, Pima-Maricopa and others call it home today, and many feel strong spiritual ties to the cliff dwellings as an ancestral home.

sites.label: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, West Fork of the Gila River, New Mexico

accounts.summary: Mogollon cliff dwellings in the Gila Wilderness, at the northern edge of the Mogollon sphere, lived in from about 1275 into the early 1300s; the Mogollon culture article dates them to the Tularosa phase. Why the community left is not known.

sites.label: Tyuonyi, Frijoles Canyon, Bandelier National Monument, New Mexico

accounts.summary: Permanent villages on the Pajarito Plateau date from 1150. Scholars believe some Ancestral Puebloan groups moved southeast into the Rio Grande valley and founded Tyuonyi, a round pueblo of one to three storeys, and the sites near it. By 1550 the settlers had moved closer to the Rio Grande; Tyuonyi was left by 1600, and its people moved to pueblos such as Cochiti and San Ildefonso, lived in ever since.

accounts.perspective: San Ildefonso Pueblo (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The people of San Ildefonso believe their ancestors lived both in the Mesa Verde area and at Bandelier.

sites.label: Pecos Pueblo, Pecos National Historical Park, New Mexico

accounts.summary: The ancestral Pecos people farmed and traded here, at Glorieta Pass between the Pueblos and the Plains, for over a thousand years; Pecos was a powerful centre of trade and culture. Their descendants still live nearby.

accounts.perspective: Archaeology and Spanish records (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The first Pecos village was one of about two dozen in the valley around 1100. Coronado's expedition visited in 1540. During the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 a kiva was built in front of the church as a rejection of the Christian religion. The last 17 or 20 people left in 1838 for Jemez Pueblo, after trying to settle at Sandia.

acoma-sky-city.title: Acoma Sky City (Haak'u)
acoma-sky-city.when: since at least 1150; lived in today (shown here to 1700)

sites.label: Acoma Pueblo (Sky City), on its mesa, New Mexico

accounts.summary: Sky City sits on a sheer-walled sandstone bluff 367 feet high. Its establishment was first recorded in 1150, and it is called the oldest continuously inhabited community in North America. Many Acoma people still live there or return for cultural occasions; the San Esteban del Rey Mission has stood among the houses since 1629.

accounts.perspective: Historians and archaeologists (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The Acoma say Sky City was founded in the 11th century, with buildings on the mesa as early as 1144; archaeologists say the pueblo had emerged by the 13th century. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in the United States.

links.title: Acoma Then & Now (Sky City Cultural Center)

old-oraibi.title: Old Oraibi (Orayvi)
old-oraibi.when: since about 1100; lived in today (shown here to 1700)

sites.label: Oraibi, Third Mesa, Hopi Reservation, Arizona

accounts.perspective: Archaeology and history (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: One of four original Hopi villages, founded about 1100, and one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the United States. Archaeologists think droughts in the late 1200s led the Hopi to leave smaller villages and gather in a few centres, Oraibi among them; it became the most influential Hopi village, with 1,500–3,000 people recorded in the 1540s.

The Hopi people have lived in Hopitutskwa since time immemorial, keeping their covenant with Maasaw to live as peaceful and humble farmers, and have kept their culture, language and religion through the centuries.

sites.label: Hawikuh Ruins, about 12 miles southwest of Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico (approximate)

accounts.summary: One of the largest Zuni towns when the Spanish came, founded about 1400; the Spanish called it Cíbola. A mission was set up in 1628–29; in 1632 the Zuni of Hawikku rose, burned the church and killed the priest. Apache raiders burned the church in 1672, and it was burned again in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, after which the Zuni left Hawikku for good.

athabaskan-arrival.title: Southern Athabaskan arrival: proposals and accounts
athabaskan-arrival.when: scholars' estimates run from before 1300 to the early 1500s

sites.label: Promontory Caves, Great Salt Lake, Utah: Dene-style moccasins dated about 1250–1290 (approximate)
Heart of Dinétah, Largo and Gobernador canyons, New Mexico: earliest dated Navajo sites, about 1500, and the Diné homeland in Diné tradition (approximate)

accounts.perspective: Linguists and archaeologists (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The Apache and Navajo speak languages of the Athabaskan family, whose other speakers live in Alaska, western Canada and the Pacific Northwest; anthropological evidence suggests their ancestors lived there before moving to the Southwest between about 1200 and 1500. Two routes are proposed: from the Great Plains, or south through the Rocky Mountains, reaching the Southwest by the 1300s or earlier. Neither rules out the other, and archaeologists find evidence of a proto-Apache presence in the southwestern mountains in the 1400s and perhaps earlier.

Most scholars think the move south began about 1000 and ended in the early 1500s, after which the Apachean groups parted; no Apachean site in the Southwest is reliably dated before 1525, but some scholars argue for 1400 or earlier. Routes proposed run through the mountains of Utah or Colorado and the Great Basin, or along the Plains close to the mountains; different groups may have used different routes. Tree-ring dates for early forked-stick hogans in northwest New Mexico fall in the late 1400s and early 1500s.

accounts.perspective: Apachean Origins Project (as reported by Archaeology, 2020)
accounts.summary: Archaeologists Jack Ives and Joel Janetski dated moccasins found at Promontory Caves, of a style Tsuut'ina elder Bruce Starlight recognises as Dene, to about 1250–1290: a few generations of Dene-speaking bison hunters, 400 years before the Spanish era. Evidence of ancestral Apachean groups in the greater Southwest as early as the 1300s is growing; Deni Seymour has studied storage sites of Dene-speaking people in southern Arizona and New Mexico. Ives: when Apache and Navajo identities emerged is still open, and 'a complex and sensitive topic for any community'.

accounts.perspective: Diné tradition (as summarised by Worley-Hood and Noyes, 2013, and Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: The Diné originated in the Four Corners region: their ancestors emerged into this world through a series of lower worlds, and the sacred mountains and rivers were made to protect the Diné. Many Navajo reject archaeologists' and anthropologists' theories of their origins because those theories contradict their oral history. Wikipedia adds that, in Diné tradition, Dinétah is also where the first four clans arrived after a migration from the north.

accounts.perspective: Adesbah Foguth, Navajo archaeologist (quoted in Archaeology, 2020)
accounts.summary: She reads the emergence through four worlds as a metaphor for stages in the growth of human consciousness: 'We evolved here, we became distinctly Navajo people here', while the people were also moving from place to place on the land. Archaeologists, she says, should listen and remember that what they have learned is one story, and that other stories are also true.

accounts.perspective: Veronica Tiller, Jicarilla Apache historian (quoted in Archaeology, 2020)
accounts.summary: Like the Navajo, the Apache tell emergence stories based in the Southwest, a coming out of the earth from darkness into light. Meeting Dene people from Canada at gatherings with the project, she found 'half of Canada related to me'; early anthropologists, she says, often missed the meaning of Jicarilla stories.

links.title: Athapaskans Arrive in the Southwest (EBSCO Research Starters)
Literature review of Utah Navajo land use (Utah Diné Bikéyah, 2013, PDF)

sites.label: Hawikuh Ruins, about 12 miles southwest of Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico (approximate)

accounts.summary: Coronado's expedition, nearly starving, reached the Zuni country looking for the 'Seven Cities of Cíbola' that Fray Marcos de Niza had reported in 1539, when Estevanico was killed at Hawikku. The Zuni refused the Spaniards entry; they attacked, met about 600 Zuni warriors, took the town and injured Coronado in the fight. Coronado admired the houses of three to five storeys but found no gold.
Some people of Hawikku escaped to the top of Dowa Yalanne, a steep mesa, where Zuni buildings served as a refuge from the Spaniards between 1540 and 1680.

sites.label: Tiguex province, the Rio Grande around Bernalillo, New Mexico (approximate; the pueblos Arenal and Moho have not been placed)

accounts.summary: Coronado's army of about 350 Spaniards and 1,300–2,000 Indigenous allies from Mexico wintered in the Tiwa towns of Tiguex, took over one pueblo (Coofor) and seized clothing and food. A Tiwa man's complaint that an officer had raped his wife went unpunished; the Tiwa killed 40 to 60 of the expedition's horses and mules, and Coronado declared war. At Arenal all the defenders were killed, about 30 of them burned at the stake after trying to surrender. The Tiwa held the mesa stronghold of Moho through an 80-day siege; their leader Xauían was killed shielding women and children as they escaped. It was the first named war between Europeans and Native Americans in what is now the United States.

The Tiwa left their towns until the expedition went on to the Plains, then gathered in fewer, larger pueblos. The Spaniards did not return for 39 years. Wikipedia names the Southern Tiwa pueblos of Sandia and Isleta, and Keres Santa Ana, as the later communities of the region.

onate-colony.title: Oñate's colony of New Mexico
onate-colony.when: 12 July 1598 (San Juan de los Caballeros); San Gabriel the capital 1601–1610; Santa Fe from 1610

sites.label: San Juan de los Caballeros, beside Ohkay Owingeh, where the Chama meets the Rio Grande (the capital moved to San Gabriel in 1601 and to Santa Fe in 1610)

accounts.summary: Juan de Oñate led 129 soldiers, 10 Franciscans, families, servants, enslaved people and livestock up the Rio Grande among about 40,000 Pueblo people, and on 12 July 1598 founded the colony at San Juan de los Caballeros beside Ohkay Owingeh. Wikipedia's article on the province says the All Pueblo Council gave the expedition permission to settle and swore loyalty to the Crown. Oñate granted colonists land and the right to demand tribute; the Pueblos had to give labour, maize and cloth, and encomiendas cut them off from farmland and water. Oñate was later tried and convicted of cruelty to natives and colonists.

accounts.perspective: Indian Pueblo Cultural Center (Jonna C. Paden, Acoma Pueblo, 2021)
accounts.summary: For over eighty years after the colony came, the Pueblo people suffered violence, cruelty and hunger, the taking of their labour and resources, and persecution for religious traditions woven into daily life.

sites.label: Acoma Pueblo (Sky City), New Mexico

accounts.perspective: Spanish records and historians (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: In December 1598 Juan de Zaldívar, Oñate's nephew, came to Acoma with soldiers for food; fighting broke out and he and eleven of his men were killed. Oñate sent Zaldívar's brother Vicente with about seventy soldiers to punish Acoma and set an example. After two days of resistance the Spaniards got a cannon onto the mesa, burned much of the town, and killed about 800 people, some 500 men and 300 women and children. About 500 were taken prisoner and tried at Ohkay Owingeh: men over 25 were sentenced to lose a foot (24 men suffered it) and to twenty years' servitude, and males of 12–25 and females over 12 to twenty years' servitude; sixty of the youngest women were sent to convents in Mexico City. Wikipedia calls it the 1599 Acoma massacre.

accounts.perspective: Acoma oral narrative (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: Acoma tradition tells that the fighting in December 1598 began when a group of Zaldívar's men attacked Acoma women while gathering corn, and Acoma warriors answered. Wikipedia's article on the massacre says the soldiers broke into homes to take maize and blankets by force.

The massacre is still a painful subject. In 1998, the 400th anniversary of the colony, a group of Acomas cut the right foot off Oñate's statue at Alcalde, 'on behalf of our brothers and sister of Acoma Pueblo'; Acoma members protested a new Oñate statue in El Paso in 2007. Survivors began rebuilding Sky City in December 1599, and it still stands.
Some writers, citing the Spanish wording, argue that the toes rather than whole feet were cut off; Wikipedia gives this as an alternative reading.

links.title: Sky City Cultural Center (Pueblo of Acoma)

sites.label: Santa Fe, besieged 13–21 August (the revolt was planned at Taos Pueblo and rose in every Pueblo town at once)

accounts.perspective: Indian Pueblo Cultural Center (Jonna C. Paden, Acoma Pueblo, 2021)
accounts.summary: On 10 August 1680 the Pueblo nations rose against the Spanish colonizers after more than eighty years of violence, hunger, forced labour and religious persecution, when talking with the Spaniards had proved useless. Each Pueblo is an autonomous nation and they had never before banded together. Po'pay ('Ripe Squash' in Tewa), a farmer of the medicine society, had been convicted of sorcery and flogged in 1675; Pueblo leaders chose him to lead. Runners carrying knotted cords to the distant Pueblos were arrested, so the revolt began early. The Spaniards could not return for twelve years, and the revolt is one reason the Pueblos still keep their lands, languages, customs and religion.

accounts.perspective: ICT (Kalle Benallie, Navajo, 2025), with Christine Sims
accounts.summary: A defining moment of Indigenous resilience, remembered every 10 August. Horses were taken, haciendas and churches destroyed, roads blocked and Santa Fe's water cut off; about 400 Spanish and others were killed and about 2,000 people left. Christine Sims (University of New Mexico) says the Spanish learned afterwards that they had to live side by side with the Pueblos and accept their self-government, languages and traditions, and that how Pueblo people recall the revolt varies by community.

accounts.perspective: Spanish records and historians (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: Po'pay won the support of Northern Tiwa, Tewa, Towa, Tano and Keres towns, Pecos, Zuni and the Hopi; the Southern Tiwa (Isleta) and the Piro did not join. About 400 colonists were killed, including 21 of the 33 Franciscans; churches at the Hopi villages were destroyed. On 21 August Governor Otermín sallied out of the besieged Palace of the Governors and then led the Spaniards south toward El Paso; the Pueblos shadowed them but did not attack. Some 1,946 survivors, about 500 of them enslaved Native people, met at Socorro. Po'pay then ordered a return to the old ways; he was deposed about a year later.

sites.label: Dowa Yalanne (Corn Mountain), about 5 km southeast of Zuni Pueblo (approximate)

accounts.summary: Before the revolt the Zuni lived in six villages. From 1680 until peace returned in 1692 they took refuge on Dowa Yalanne ('Corn Mountain'), a steep mesa; afterwards they settled at Halona, today's Zuni Pueblo, returning to the mesa only briefly in 1703.

sites.label: Santa Fe

accounts.perspective: Spanish records and historians (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: Diego de Vargas came to Santa Fe with about sixty soldiers, a hundred Native auxiliaries and seven cannon, and promised the thousand Pueblo people there clemency if they swore allegiance to the King and returned to the Church. After first refusing, they agreed, and on 14 September he proclaimed a formal act of repossession, then visited other Pueblos. The Hopi kept their independence.

accounts.perspective: Pueblo tribal history (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: In 1691 or 1692 a delegation from Jemez, Zia, Santa Ana, San Felipe, Pecos and several Tano towns went to Guadalupe del Paso and, according to tribal history, invited the Spaniards to return, at a time of hunger and raids.

accounts.perspective: Native protest today (as summarised by Wikipedia)
accounts.summary: In the 2010s Native people protested the Entrada, a re-enactment of Vargas's entry in the Fiestas de Santa Fe that historians called inaccurate and Native Americans offensive; it was dropped from the fiesta.

santa-fe-1693.title: Vargas retakes Santa Fe by force

sites.label: Santa Fe

accounts.summary: Vargas came back with about 800 colonists and 100 soldiers. Seventy Pueblo warriors and 400 of their families in the town refused them entry; after a quick, bloody fight the warriors surrendered and were executed on 30 December, and about 400 women and children were sentenced to ten years' servitude among the colonists. A second revolt by fourteen pueblos in 1696 was put down harshly, and by 1700 the reconquest was all but complete.

sites.label: Taenhatentaron (Saint-Ignace) and Saint-Louis, Tay Township near Midland (approximate)

accounts.summary: Haudenosaunee warriors took the mission villages of Saint-Ignace and Saint-Louis. The Jesuit missionaries Jean de Brébeuf and Gabriel Lalemant were captured there and killed.

The attacks of 1648–49 broke the Wendat confederacy. Within weeks the Wendat abandoned their villages, and by 1650 they had dispersed: some to Gahoendoe (Christian Island), some to Québec, some to join the Haudenosaunee, and others west.

sites.label: Gahoendoe (Christian Island), Sainte-Marie II

accounts.summary: Wendat refugees, Jesuits and French soldiers built a fortified mission, Sainte-Marie II, on the island. Famine and disease killed many in the winter of 1649–50. In June 1650 about 300 Wendat left with the Jesuits for Québec, where the Huron-Wendat Nation lives at Wendake today.

sites.label: Attawandaron country, Grand River to Niagara (approximate)

accounts.summary: The French called the Attawandaron 'Neutral' because they kept out of the wars between the Wendat and the Haudenosaunee. After the Wendat dispersal the Haudenosaunee went to war with them about 1650, and by 1651 they had dispersed; war, disease and famine all played a part. The last mention of them as an independent people is in 1653.

sites.label: Erie country, south shore of Lake Erie (the fort's site is not known)

accounts.summary: Seneca and Onondaga warriors besieged a large Erie fort in the summer of 1654 and took it. By 1656 the Erie no longer existed as a political body; survivors were killed, scattered or taken captive, and most were absorbed into Haudenosaunee communities.
In November 1655 the Jesuits recorded the execution of Erie captives.

north-shore-villages-1667.title: Haudenosaunee villages founded on the north shore of Lake Ontario

sites.label: Quinaouatoua (Tinawatawa), near Hamilton
Teiaiagon, Humber River (Baby Point, Toronto)
Ganatsekwyagon, mouth of the Rouge River
Ganaraske, Port Hope
Kentsio, Rice Lake (approximate)
Kente, Bay of Quinte (approximate)
Ganneious, near Napanee (exact site unknown)

accounts.summary: By the late 1660s the Five Nations had seven villages on the shores of Lake Ontario, near the portages that led north. Teiaiagon is described as Seneca (with Mohawk), and Ganneious as Oneida.

accounts.perspective: Why they were built: interpretations differ
accounts.summary: Some accounts describe the villages as bases for hunting beaver and controlling the flow of furs to Albany. Jon Parmenter reads them instead as a return to ancestral lands.

sites.label: Point Iroquois, on Lake Superior near the outlet to the St. Marys River

accounts.summary: Later Ojibwe accounts name Point Iroquois as the site of the last great Ojibwe–Iroquois battle in the Ojibwe heartland; the place was earlier called the Grave of the Iroquois because so many died there.
Perrot described the Iroquois defeat, adding the caution that, although the Iroquois were said not to have dared enter Lake Superior again, in truth they never set themselves any limits.

sites.label: Ganondagan, Seneca town near Victor, New York
Kente and Ganneious, north shore of Lake Ontario: villages destroyed, 200 prisoners taken (June 1687)

accounts.summary: The Marquis de Denonville led about 1,600 colonial troops, militia and Native allies. After a short fight near Ganondagan the Seneca withdrew; the French found the town already burned and destroyed the stored and standing corn of four Seneca towns. Denonville reported 45 Seneca killed.
The Seneca had moved their families to Cayuga and burned their own towns as the women and children fled. This report describes the Seneca force differently, and the casualty figures are disputed.
All seven Haudenosaunee villages on the north shore of Lake Ontario were abandoned after 1687.

battle-of-the-skulls.title: Battle of the Skulls (Skull Mound)
battle-of-the-skulls.when: 1690s, by oral tradition; the accounts give no exact date

sites.label: Mouth of the Saugeen River: Copway places Skull Mound at a principal Iroquois village here
Blue Mountains, south of Georgian Bay: the Odawa writer Assikinack's account (Eid places it near Penetanguishene)
An island in lower Georgian Bay, afterwards called Pequahkoondebaminis, the island of skulls: the Paudash account (the island is not identified; marker is approximate)

accounts.perspective: Ojibwe tradition, written by George Copway (1850)
accounts.summary: An Anishinaabe army divided to attack on several fronts. One force, heading south to meet Wendat allies, attacked a principal Iroquois village on the Saugeen River. The dead were buried in mounds that the painter Paul Kane still saw, with scattered bones, in the mid-1800s. The combined forces then overran the whole southern peninsula.

accounts.perspective: Mississauga tradition: Robert and Johnson Paudash (sworn statement, 1904)
accounts.summary: Handed down from Robert Paudash's father and grandfather. A Mohawk party entrenched on an island in lower Georgian Bay was surrounded and destroyed, and the island was afterwards named for the skulls. The Mississaugas then drove the Mohawks south through the Trent valley and carried the war to the Mohawk River, where peace was made.

Ojibwe forces from Lake Superior joined Odawa from Manitoulin Island at the Blue Mountains. Scouts at Rice Lake warned of an Iroquois war party; Ojibwe from the Saugeen River and Owen Sound came in, and the Iroquois were almost annihilated, a few being sent home to tell of the defeat.

accounts.perspective: Haudenosaunee tradition, written by David Cusick (Tuscarora, 1827)
accounts.summary: The Mississaugas, whom Cusick calls Twakanhah, made war on the Five Nations, and the Seneca on the frontier bore the brunt. After skirmishes the enemy tried and failed to destroy a fort near present-day Lewiston; Seneca parties went by canoe to the head of Lake Ontario in search of them, and a Five Nations army of two thousand withdrew after a hard fight with a strong enemy force. Eid notes that Cusick's dates are unreliable.
In June 1700 Haudenosaunee envoys told the English commissioners at Albany that they had given the Mississaugas permission to settle at Toronto, presenting the move as their own grant.

Leroy Eid argues that the Anishinaabe accounts agree with one another and with colonial records, and that the Five Nations lost this war. Many earlier historians held that the Haudenosaunee remained the dominant power; José António Brandão describes them making peace at Montreal in 1701 after failing to dislodge the French.

trent-valley-1690s.title: Battles along the Trent valley (Mississauga tradition)

sites.label: Nogojiwanong (Peterborough): a skirmish at Cemetery Point
Rice Lake: a major battle, the Mohawks driven to Rochis Point (marker approximate)
Onigaming, the carrying place between Lake Ontario and the Bay of Quinte

accounts.perspective: Mississauga tradition: Robert and Johnson Paudash (sworn statement, 1904)
accounts.summary: After the battle in Georgian Bay the Mississaugas came south by the Severn River and the Narrows of Lake Simcoe. The Mohawks retreated down the Otonabee and the Trent: there was fighting at Peterborough, a great battle at Rice Lake, and further fighting at the foot of the lake and at the carrying place to the Bay of Quinte. The Mississaugas then settled the Trent valley.
Eid notes that the Paudash account parallels Copway's in describing a planned campaign that divided and reunited, ending in the Haudenosaunee homeland.

sites.label: Albany, New York

accounts.summary: The Five Nations placed a vast 'beaver hunting ground', including southern Ontario and lands west to present-day Chicago, under the protection of the English Crown, claiming it by right of conquest in the Beaver Wars. The French did not recognise the grant. Anishinaabe peoples were moving into southern Ontario at the same time.

sites.label: Montreal

accounts.summary: About 1,300 delegates of some 39 nations made peace with New France and with one another, among them the Five Nations, the Wendat, Odawa, Ojibwe and Algonquin, with the Mississaugas represented by a Potawatomi speaker. The Haudenosaunee promised to stay neutral in wars between the French and English colonies, and disputes were to be settled by negotiation, with the French as arbiters.
Eid reads the treaty as the end of Haudenosaunee dominance in the region. Brandão describes the Haudenosaunee making peace after failing to dislodge the French.

sites.label: Fort Niagara

accounts.summary: Sir William Johnson met representatives of 24 nations. They ratified the Royal Proclamation of 1763, the Covenant Chain of friendship was extended into the Great Lakes, and a four-mile strip on the west bank of the Niagara River was transferred. The agreement was recorded in wampum; no paper treaty was signed. Some nations, including the Wyandot of Sandusky and the Lenape and Shawnee of Ohio, refused to attend.

sites.label: Fort Stanwix, near Rome, New York

accounts.summary: Britain and the Six Nations agreed a Line of Property running from near Fort Pitt down the Ohio River to the Tennessee River. Lands south and east of it, including Kentucky and most of present-day West Virginia, were ceded to the Crown.

haldimand-1784.title: Haldimand Proclamation: the Grand River grant

sites.label: Grand River, Ontario

accounts.summary: Governor Frederick Haldimand granted the Mohawk and other Six Nations people who wished to settle there the land six miles deep on each side of the Grand River, from Lake Erie to its source. The Crown had bought the land from the Mississaugas in May 1784.

links.title: Six Nations of the Grand River

kittanning-1724.title: Lenape found Kittanning on the Allegheny

sites.label: Kittanning, on the Allegheny River

accounts.summary: After the Beaver Wars the Ohio country was largely uninhabited for decades and served as Haudenosaunee hunting ground. Peoples began returning in the 1720s: the Lenape founded Kittanning by 1724, and Shawnee and other eastern bands followed.

sites.label: Pickawillany, on the Great Miami River near Piqua, Ohio

accounts.summary: Memeskia (Old Briton) had led Miami families from Kekionga in 1747 and traded with the English; by 1750 the town held about 400 families. Charles de Langlade led about 240 French-allied Odawa warriors against it while most men were away, killed Memeskia and an English trader, and burned the trading post. It is seen as a prelude to the French and Indian War.

sites.label: Fort Detroit

accounts.summary: A coalition led by the Odawa leader Pontiac besieged Detroit for six months; eight British forts fell in 1763, and Detroit and Fort Pitt were besieged. News of the rising led to the Royal Proclamation of October 1763, which drew a line between the colonies and Indian lands. Pontiac made peace with Sir William Johnson in July 1766 without ceding land.

sites.label: Gnadenhutten, a Moravian mission village on the Tuscarawas River

accounts.summary: About 160 Pennsylvania militiamen under David Williamson lured the Christian Lenape and Mohican of the mission in with promises of safe relocation, accused them of raiding, voted to kill them, and killed 96 people: 28 men, 29 women and 39 children. Two boys survived. Eighteen militiamen refused to take part.

st-clair-1791.title: Battle of the Wabash (St. Clair's defeat)

sites.label: Fort Recovery, Ohio

accounts.summary: A confederacy led by Little Turtle (Miami), Blue Jacket (Shawnee) and Buckongahelas (Lenape) routed Arthur St. Clair's army advancing on Kekionga. Several hundred Americans were killed; Native losses were about sixty. It is counted as the worst defeat of a United States army by Native nations.

sites.label: Near Maumee, Ohio, by the Maumee River

accounts.summary: Anthony Wayne's Legion defeated a confederacy of about 1,500 warriors under Blue Jacket, Buckongahelas, Little Turtle, Tarhe and others in a fight of about an hour. The British commander of nearby Fort Miami shut the gates on the retreating warriors to avoid war with the United States. Wayne then burned towns along the Maumee.

sites.label: Fort Greenville, Ohio

accounts.summary: The Wyandot, Lenape, Shawnee, Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Miami and others ceded about two-thirds of the Ohio country, south and east of a line from the mouth of the Cuyahoga to Fort Recovery and on to the Ohio River, in return for goods worth $20,000 and annual payments.
